name: What Changes at Every Hop
brief:
This is the U4 mastery gate, and it is not a typing exercise. Send one packet from PC1 to PC2, then open the packet inspector and read what happened at each hop.

The question the competition asks in a dozen different wordings is always the same: which addresses change as a packet crosses a router, and which ones do not?
watchFor: Layer 2 addresses are rewritten at every hop. Layer 3 addresses are the same at the first hop and the last. If your answers do not show that pattern, look again.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping PC2 at 192.168.20.20 so there is a packet to inspect.
In the inspector, read the SOURCE IP address of the packet as it leaves R1 toward R2.
tasks.hint: Layer 3 addressing is end to end.

tasks.text: Read the DESTINATION IP address of that same packet.
Read the SOURCE MAC address of that frame. Which device does it belong to?
tasks.hint: The frame leaving R1 on G0/1 carries R1 G0/1 as its source. Not PC1.

tasks.text: Read the DESTINATION MAC address of that frame. Which device does it belong to?
On PC1, run arp -a. Confirm PC1 knows the gateway MAC and does NOT know PC2 MAC.
tasks.hint: You ARP for the gateway, not for the far host. PC1 has never needed PC2 hardware address and never will.

tasks.text: Confirm PC1 has no ARP entry for 192.168.20.20.

extension: Now answer the same four questions for the LAST hop, from R2 to PC2, without looking at the inspector. Then check yourself.
debrief:
Say it in one sentence and you own the unit: the IP addresses identify the endpoints and never change; the MAC addresses identify the next device on this wire and are rewritten every hop.

Everything about ARP follows from that. A host ARPs for the gateway because the gateway is the next device on its wire, not because the gateway is the destination.
